## Introduction

In this 10-minute activity, you first check that your result
reproduces, then change one input, predict what needs rebuilding,
and update the report. By the end, you should be able to explain how
the pipeline and report keep a reported result consistent with its
inputs.

Continue in the same session with your completed
`workspace/_targets.R` and `workspace/report.qmd`.
[Report checkpoint](06_quarto.qmd#quarto-checkpoint)

## Step 1: reproduce the result

Allow about three minutes. In the **R Console**, keep a copy of the
current summary, ask *targets* to forget that every target is up to
date, and rebuild everything from the pinned input. This is what
happens when a collaborator runs the pipeline for the first time.

```{r health-modify-setup, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
box::use(
  targets[everything, tar_invalidate, tar_make, tar_outdated, tar_read],
  utils[read.csv]
)

workshop_dir <- file.path("outputs", "health-wellbeing")
pipeline_script <- file.path("workspace", "_targets.R")
pipeline_store <- file.path(workshop_dir, "_targets")
selection_file <- file.path(workshop_dir, "analysis-data-version.txt")
summary_path <- file.path(workshop_dir, "meta-summary.csv")
stopifnot(file.exists(pipeline_script), file.exists(summary_path))
```

```{r health-modify-reproduce, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
before <- read.csv(summary_path)
tar_invalidate(everything(), store = pipeline_store)
tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
after <- read.csv(summary_path)
identical(before, after)
```

`tar_invalidate()` removes the records that mark targets as up to
date; it does not delete the pinned data. Every target reruns, and
`TRUE` means the rebuilt summary matches the previous one exactly in
this environment. Another R or *meta* version could change the final
digits, which is why the summary records both.

## Step 2: change the input

Allow about three minutes. Before running anything, predict which
targets will be outdated if the selection file names the
general-population version instead of the full dataset. Then switch
the selection and check your prediction.

```{r health-modify-select-general, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
versions <- read.csv(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "dataset-versions.csv"),
  colClasses = "character"
)
general_version <- versions$version[versions$scope == "general"]
stopifnot(length(general_version) == 1L)
writeLines(general_version, selection_file)

tar_outdated(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
```

Every target is outdated: the selection file is the first step, and
all later steps depend on it. Rebuild and read the new result.

```{r health-modify-rebuild-general, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_read(result, store = pipeline_store)[
  , c("data_version", "studies", "pooled_r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")
]
```

## Step 3: update the report

Allow about two minutes. In the **Terminal**, at the project root,
render the report again and reload it in your browser.

```bash
quarto render workspace/report.qmd --to html
```

The report now describes 18 studies and names the general-population
pin version in its provenance. You did not edit a single number by
hand. The subset's pooled correlation is similar, with a wider
interval from fewer studies. It is a planned teaching comparison, not
a replacement for the full analysis.

## Step 4: restore the full dataset

Allow about two minutes. Select the full version again, rebuild, and
check that nothing is outdated.

```{r health-modify-restore, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
full_version <- versions$version[versions$scope == "all"]
stopifnot(length(full_version) == 1L)
writeLines(full_version, selection_file)

tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_outdated(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
tar_read(result, store = pipeline_store)$studies
```

*targets* keeps only the latest result for each target, so switching
back reruns the steps. Render the report once more so it matches the
full analysis.

## Optional: change a method instead

If you have time, make a code change rather than a data change. In
`workspace/_targets.R`, step 5, change `method.tau = "REML"` to
`method.tau = "DL"`, the DerSimonian–Laird estimator, and save the
file.

Predict the outdated targets, then run `tar_outdated()`. Only `fit`,
`result`, and `summary_file` are listed, because the input steps have
not changed. Run `tar_make()` and render the report. Its Methods
section now names the DerSimonian–Laird method, and the pooled
correlation stays at about 0.363. This is a quick sensitivity check:
the result does not depend on this choice of estimator. Change the
setting back to `"REML"` and rebuild before you finish.

In your own project, the pipeline would be a tracked file. `git diff`
would show the one-line change, and a commit would record why you made
it.

## Checkpoint {#modify-checkpoint}

-   Rebuilding from the pinned input gave an identical summary.
-   With the general-population version, the pipeline combined **18
    studies** with a pooled correlation of about **0.38** and a 95%
    interval of about **0.30 to 0.45**, and the report updated without
    manual edits.
-   After restoring the full version, `tar_outdated()` is empty and the
    summary shows 29 studies again.
-   You can explain why a data change reruns every target, while a
    method change reruns only the model and its outputs.
